806.title: Baba Buddha
806.hook: the boy Nanak met lived to serve six Gurus and, tradition says, applied the tilak to their successors
806.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Baba Buddha as a model of lifelong seva, and gurdwaras connected with his memory, including Gurdwara Bir Baba Buddha Sahib, draw visitors who come to remember his service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Khivi: shade like a leafy tree, kheer made with ghee, and your line, generous kitchen. Today, a boy with the cattle.

A boy is out with the cattle when a holy man passes on the road. He could have kept his eyes on the herd. Instead he brings milk, sits down, and asks a question that sounds far too old for him: how do I escape death? The holy man asks why a boy so young is thinking about that. The boy's answer, as Sikhs tell it, earned him a new name for the rest of his life.
screen: `A BOY WITH THE CATTLE.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DEATH.` → `AN ANSWER THAT EARNED A NAME.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sikh tradition. The boy, named Bura, tells Guru Nanak what he saw at home. When his mother lights the cooking fire, she doesn't start with the big logs. She starts with the small twigs, and they burn up first. So, he says, if the small ones go first in the fire, who's to say death will wait for the old? Guru Nanak, the story says, answered that he spoke like an old man, a buddha, a wise elder. And the name stuck: Baba Buddha. Then comes the long part. That boy, tradition says, lived to serve six Gurus, from Guru Nanak on. When guruship passed from one Guru to the next, tradition says it was Baba Buddha who applied the tilak, the mark on the forehead, to the new Guru. The hands that once herded cattle by the road marked Guru after Guru, across a lifetime. Sikh tradition remembers him at the Harmandir Sahib too: when Guru Arjan installed the Granth there, tradition says Baba Buddha was asked to read from it. Through all of it, the stories don't make him a leader who sought power. He's honored for service. He tended, he read, he marked, he stayed. The name came first, from a boy watching twigs catch in his mother's fire; the long life of service came after. Sikhs remember the two together: a child who spoke like an elder, and an elder who kept serving like that same attentive boy, one Guru after another.

807.title: Bibi Amro
807.hook: Guru Angad's daughter whose dawn singing brought Amar Das to the Guru
807.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Amro in the story of how Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad, and some Sikh households still sing gurbani during ordinary work, at home and at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Buddha, the boy who, tradition says, lived to serve one Guru after another; your line was six gurus served. Today, a song before sunrise.

It's still dark. In a village house, a young woman sits at the churn, pulling the cord back and forth, turning milk into butter the way it was done every morning. While her hands work, she sings, just enough to keep time with the churn. On the other side of the wall, an older man in the same family is awake too. He's devout, and tradition says he has walked to the holy river many times in his life, still looking for something. He hears the words. He stops. And he asks a question that will change the rest of his life: whose words are these?
screen: `STILL DARK, A CHURN, A SONG.` → `AN OLDER MAN LISTENING.` → `WHOSE WORDS ARE THESE?`

segments.voice: Bibi Amro was the daughter of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who sat in Guru Nanak's seat at Khadur. Tradition says she married into the family of a man named Amar Das and went to live in his village. Amar Das was religious in the way of his time: he kept fasts, went on pilgrimage, was good and careful. But the story says he had never had a teacher. Then one morning he heard his young relative singing at her work, a hymn of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the words went straight into him. He asked whose they were. She told him plainly: these are Guru Nanak's words, and my father now sits in his place. Amar Das asked her to take him there, and she did. She brought him to Khadur, to her father, and he never really left. The story says he stayed to serve Guru Angad for years, carrying water, doing the plain work of the house. And in time, Guru Angad chose him to be the next Guru: Guru Amar Das, the third. Notice what Bibi Amro did, and what she didn't. She didn't argue with him. She didn't set out to convince anybody. She was churning butter, and the song was part of her morning, as ordinary as the milk. Because it was real to her, it carried through a wall. Sikhs remember her for faith that simply sounded while she worked. One woman singing at dawn, and the Guruship found its next keeper.

808.title: Bibi Bhani
808.hook: daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third; tradition says she once held her father's stool steady with her hand
808.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Bhani as the daughter of Guru Amar Das, wife of Guru Ram Das and mother of Guru Arjan, and tell the story of the broken stool as an example of quiet, steady service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Amro sang at the churn, and Amar Das heard Guru Nanak's words through the wall; your line was her song changed a life. Today, Guru Amar Das's own daughter.

A low wooden stool: short legs, a flat seat, the kind every household had and nobody looked at twice. Tradition says Guru Amar Das sat on one like it each morning while he bathed and prayed. One morning, a leg gave way. Nobody in the story makes a speech or calls for a carpenter. His daughter is there, and she does the only thing there's time to do. She slides her hand under the broken corner and holds the seat level, so her father's stillness isn't broken.
screen: `A LOW WOODEN STOOL.` → `ONE LEG GIVES WAY.` → `A HAND UNDER THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Bibi Bhani's family tree reads like a list of the Gurus. She was the daughter of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. She married Bhai Jetha, a young man from Lahore who served in her father's house, and he became Guru Ram Das, the fourth. Their son became Guru Arjan, the fifth. Daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third. Now the stool. Tradition tells it this way. The leg broke while her father sat in prayer, and Bibi Bhani put her hand beneath the seat and held it. She held it so long, the story says, that the wood cut her hand and it bled. She didn't move, and she didn't call out. When Guru Amar Das opened his eyes, he saw the blood on the floor and understood. Tradition says he was moved, and told her to ask for something. She didn't ask for jewelry, or rest, or praise. She asked that the Guruship stay in her household. Sikh tradition reads what followed through that moment: from her husband onward, the Gurus came from her family line. Some tellings say her father warned her the gift would come with suffering, and Sikhs remember that it did. So the story holds two things: devotion that doesn't need an audience, and steadiness as a kind of strength. Holding something level is quiet work. Nobody claps for it. But a whole household, and in this story a whole line of Gurus, can rest on a hand that doesn't let go.

809.title: Mata Ganga
809.hook: Guru Arjan's wife, who, tradition says, walked to Baba Buddha with simple bread and onions to ask for a son's blessing
809.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Mata Ganga's visit to Baba Buddha as a lesson in humility: the blessing came when she walked there with bread she had made herself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Bhani held her father's broken stool level until her hand bled; your line was she held it steady. Today, her daughter-in-law.

What do you bring to someone whose blessing you want? One instinct is to bring the best: the good dishes, the nicest clothes, a little ceremony to show you mean it. That's exactly what Mata Ganga did the first time. Tradition says she set out with attendants, a carriage and fine food, to visit an old man who lived out among the fields and cattle. She came home with nothing. The second time, she walked.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU BRING?` → `THE FIRST TIME: CARRIAGE AND FINE FOOD.` → `THE SECOND TIME: SHE WALKED.`

segments.voice: Mata Ganga was the wife of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, Bibi Bhani's son. Tradition says that for a long time the couple had no child, and Mata Ganga longed for a son. Guru Arjan, the story goes, sent her to Baba Buddha, the old Sikh who had known Guru Nanak and now tended the Guru's fields and herds. So she went the way a Guru's wife might be expected to: carriage, servants, rich dishes, the dust of the procession rolling up the road. Baba Buddha, tradition says, asked what all the commotion was about, and gave no blessing. She went home disappointed. Guru Arjan didn't scold her. He suggested another way. This time she ground the flour and kneaded the dough herself. She made plain bread, the kind farm workers eat, took onions and buttermilk with it, and went on foot, alone or nearly so. Baba Buddha was hungry from the work, and glad. He sat and ate. Then, tradition says, he crushed an onion in his fist and said her son would be strong enough to crush the pride of tyrants the same way. Sikhs say the son born to her was Guru Hargobind, the Guru remembered for taking up the sword alongside the Name. So what changed? Not the request. Not the person. Only how she came. With the carriage, she arrived as someone important. With the bread, she arrived as someone asking. The story says the blessing waited for the second.

810.title: Bhai Gurdas, the man
810.hook: the scribe who, tradition says, was once tested and forgiven by Guru Hargobind
810.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Granth and the author of the Vars, which are sung in gurdwaras, and they tell the story of his test and forgiveness as part of who he was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Ganga walked to Baba Buddha with bread she'd made herself; your line was simple bread, big blessing. Today, a man the path has met before, seen up close.

A letter arrives at a king's court in Banaras, far from Punjab. It's from Guru Hargobind, and it says something strange: a thief of mine is hiding in your city. Find him, tie his hands, and send him back to me. The king's men go looking. Before they find anyone, a quiet, learned man steps forward and says: that's me. I'm the one he means. The thief is the Guru's own scribe.
screen: `A LETTER TO BANARAS.` → `FIND MY THIEF AND TIE HIS HANDS.` → `THAT'S ME.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas is a name this path has met as a writer. Tradition says he wrote out the Granth as Guru Arjan dictated it, and Sikhs speak of his own Vars as a key to the Guru's word. So it's a surprise that the story Sikhs tell about him as a man is a story of failure. There's more than one version. In a well-known one, Guru Hargobind sent him to Kabul with money to buy horses. He made the bargain and went into his tent to fetch the payment, and the money wasn't there. Some tellings say it had turned to stones. With the dealers waiting outside, he panicked. He was the Guru's trusted man, and he couldn't pay. So he slipped out the back of the tent and ran, all the way to Banaras, where nobody knew him. Some tellings add a reason for the test: he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver. Then came the letter about the thief. He knew at once who was meant. He gave himself up and was led back with his hands tied. Before Guru Hargobind, tradition says, he answered in verse, admitting he had failed and asking for mercy the way a child asks a parent. The Guru forgave him, and he stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life. Sikhs didn't hide this story to protect a great name. They kept it. The man tradition credits with writing out the Granth was tested, ran, came back, and was forgiven.

811.title: Bhai Bidhi Chand
811.hook: a former thief turned Sikh, famous in tradition for recovering the Guru's horses from Lahore in disguise
811.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Bidhi Chand as one of the companions of Guru Hargobind, remembered for his courage and cleverness after he left a life of theft and came to the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Gurdas ran to Banaras, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven; your line was even he was tested. Today, a man whose past was worse than one lapse.

Some skills don't look good on a résumé. Moving without a sound. Reading a guard's habits. Talking your way past a gate. Getting out of a place before anyone notices you're gone. Bhai Bidhi Chand had all of them, and Sikh tradition doesn't pretend otherwise: before he came to the Guru, he was a thief. The surprise is what happened to those skills afterward. They didn't vanish. They changed owners.
screen: `SKILLS THAT DON'T LOOK GOOD ON A RÉSUMÉ.` → `HE WAS A THIEF.` → `THE SKILLS CHANGED OWNERS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bidhi Chand grew up in a village near Amritsar and fell in with bad company, stealing to live. Then he came into the Guru's circle in the time of Guru Arjan, and his life turned. He became a Sikh, and later one of Guru Hargobind's trusted companions. Now his famous story. Tradition says devoted Sikhs from far to the west were bringing fine horses as an offering to Guru Hargobind, and on the road, officials seized them and sent them to the royal stables in Lahore Fort. Tradition names the horses Dilbagh and Gulbagh. The Guru's people were upset, and Bidhi Chand said, in effect: leave this to me. He went to Lahore dressed as a grass-cutter, and sold the stables grass so good and so cheap that they hired him to tend the horses. He was patient. He won the grooms' trust. Every night, the story says, he threw a heavy stone off the fort wall into the river below, until the guards grew used to the splash and stopped looking. Then one night, the splash was him. He rode the horse over the wall into the water, swam it across, and brought it to the Guru. For the second horse, tradition says, he came back as a fortune-teller who claimed he could find what had been stolen, and rode off with that one too. Sikhs tell this with a grin. Under the grin is something serious: the Guru didn't ask Bidhi Chand to become a different man with no past. He took the cleverness, the nerve, the patience, and turned them toward something true.

812.title: Mian Mir
812.hook: a Sufi saint of Lahore who was Guru Arjan's friend; tradition says he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone
812.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor as Guru Arjan's friend, and the story that he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone is often told at the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Bidhi Chand turned a thief's nerve to the Guru's service; your line was a thief turned true. Today, Lahore again, and a very different man.

The week ends here, so first, a roll call of the faces around the Gurus. Baba Buddha, who served Guru after Guru. Bibi Amro, singing at the churn. Bibi Bhani, her hand under a broken stool. Mata Ganga, walking with plain bread. Bhai Gurdas, the scribe who ran and came back. Bhai Bidhi Chand, over the wall. Every one a Sikh, or a Guru's family. And the last face of the week, standing beside Guru Arjan at the edge of a pool in Amritsar, isn't a Sikh at all.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF THE WEEK.` → `SIKHS AND THE GURUS' FAMILY.` → `THE LAST FACE ISN'T A SIKH.`

segments.voice: Mian Mir was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, who lived in Lahore. Tradition remembers him for a plain life of prayer and for the company he kept, which included Guru Arjan. They were friends: not allies in a debate, not rivals being polite, but friends who visited and talked about God. When Guru Arjan was building the Harmandir, the house of God in the middle of the pool at Amritsar, tradition says he invited Mian Mir to lay its foundation stone. Some historians question whether it happened that way. Sikhs still tell it, and it's easy to hear why: a Sikh house of worship, its first stone set by a Muslim friend. That fits the building itself. The Harmandir sits low, so you step down to enter it, and it has doors on every side, open to anyone coming from any direction. There's a harder story too. When Guru Arjan was arrested and tortured in Lahore, tradition says Mian Mir came to him, grieving, and offered to intervene. Guru Arjan, the story says, asked him not to: this was God's will, and he accepted it. Mian Mir stayed a friend to the end, and the Guru stayed himself. Neither man became the other. Mian Mir didn't become a Sikh; Guru Arjan didn't become a Sufi. Each stood fully in his own path, and they were close anyway. Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor, and his shrine in Lahore is still visited.
